title: Barefoot in Treichville
author: Léxi
desc: Koffi joue au foot pieds nus dans la rue. Un recruteur arrive… le jour où il se blesse.

p: In Treichville, there is no stadium for children. There is only a dusty street, two stones for the goal, and a ball that is more tape than ball.
Koffi is fourteen. He plays every evening, barefoot. He is small and thin, but when he has the ball, nobody can stop him. He turns left, he turns right, and the older boys fall on the ground.
"Koffi! Koffi!" the little children shout.
His grandmother does not like football. "Football doesn't feed a family," she says. "Study, my son. Study."
Koffi loves his grandmother. He studies. But every evening, when the sun goes down, his feet go back to the street.

chapters.t: The Man in the Red Cap
p: One Saturday, a man in a red cap stands near the street. He watches the game for one hour. He writes things in a small notebook.
"Who is he?" asks Koffi's friend Ibou.
"A recruiter," says an older boy. "From an academy. They look for new players."
Koffi's heart beats fast. He plays the best game of his life. He scores three goals. The man in the red cap smiles.
After the game, the man comes to him. "My name is Coach Diomandé. Next Saturday, we have a test at the academy in Yopougon. Come. Bring shoes."
Koffi has no football shoes. He has no money. But he says: "I'll be there."
On Wednesday, three days before the test, Koffi plays in the street. A big boy pushes him. He falls on a stone. His ankle hurts terribly.
At home, his ankle is big and blue. His grandmother puts ice and leaves on it.
"No football for two weeks," she says.
Koffi cries in his bed. Two weeks. The test is on Saturday. His chance is gone.
That night, his grandmother sits next to him. She is quiet for a long time.
"Your grandfather played football too," she says finally. "He was very good. But one day, he was injured, and he never tried again. All his life, he was sad about it."
Koffi looks at her, surprised. She never talks about his grandfather.
"Don't do the same thing," she says. "If one door closes, knock on it again."
On Saturday, Koffi goes to the academy with his grandmother. He can walk, but he cannot run.
He finds Coach Diomandé and tells him the truth. "I'm injured. I can't play today. But please, don't forget me."
The coach looks at the ankle. He looks at the old grandmother who came by bus with her grandson. Then he does something surprising. He laughs.
"Do you know how many boys lie to me? They play injured and they hurt themselves more. You told me the truth. That is the first quality of a great player."
He writes in his notebook. "Come back in one month. And here." He gives Koffi a box. Inside, there are new football shoes.
On the bus home, Koffi holds the box on his knees all the way. His grandmother sleeps on his shoulder.
One month later, Koffi plays at the academy test. He doesn't score three goals. He scores one. But he runs everywhere, he helps every player, and he never stops.
At the end, Coach Diomandé shakes his hand. "Welcome to the academy, Koffi. Training every day after school. And your school results must stay good. That is the rule."
Koffi runs home. Well, he walks fast, because his ankle is still a little weak.
"Grandma! I'm in! I'm in the academy!"
His grandmother puts down her pot. She doesn't say *football doesn't feed a family.* She takes his face in her hands.
"Your grandfather is smiling today," she says.

The next evening, Koffi goes back to the dusty street in Treichville. The little children run to him. He takes off his new shoes, and he plays barefoot with them until the sun goes down. Because some things must never change.
